sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
A set [MATH: A] is countably infinite (or denumerable) if [MATH: |A| = |\mathbb{N}|.] A set is countable if it is either finite or countably infinite.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

  • Statement I is false. The set [MATH: A] has infinitely many elements.

  • Statement II is true. Indeed, [MATH: A|= {(− 2)^{n}∣n ∈ N}; = {− 2, 4, − 8, 16, − 32…}] can be represented as a (one-way infinite) sequence. So, it's countably infinite (or denumerable).

  • Statement III is true since any countably infinite set is also countable.

  • Statement IV is false since statement III is true.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

> The union of two countably infinite sets is countably infinite.

Content:
This property can be generalized to the union of any number of countably infinite sets and even to the union of countably many countably infinite sets:

Content:
> The union of countably many countably infinite sets is countably infinite.

Content:
We can express this result as follows:

Content:
> If [MATH: |A_i| = \aleph_0] for all natural [MATH: i,] then [MATH: \displaystyle \bigg| \bigcup_{i=1}^\infty A_i \bigg| = \aleph_0.]

Content:
If we combine "fewer" sets (e.g., a finite number), or if some of the [MATH: A_i]'s are finite, the resulting union must also be countable.

Given the set [MATH: A] above, which of the following statements are true?

1. [MATH: |A| = 2]
2. [MATH: |A| = |\mathbb{Z}|]
3. [MATH: |A \cup \mathbb{Z}| =|\mathbb{N}|]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Recall that the union of a finite set and a countably infinite set is countably infinite.

Also, note that

  • [MATH: A =\{-3, 3\}] is finite with [MATH: |A|=2,] and

  • [MATH: \mathbb{N}] and [MATH: \mathbb{Z}] are countably infinite with the same cardinality.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

  • Statement I is true. The set [MATH: A] is finite with [MATH: |A|=2.]

  • Statement II is false. The set [MATH: A] is finite with [MATH: |A|=2.] On the other hand, [MATH: \mathbb{Z}] is infinite with [MATH: |\mathbb{Z}|=\aleph_0.] So, [MATH: | A | =2 \neq \aleph_0 = |\mathbb{Z}|.]

  • Statement III is true. The set [MATH: A] is finite, while [MATH: |\mathbb{Z}| = \aleph_0.] As a result, [MATH: |A \cup \mathbb{Z}| = \aleph_0.] On the other hand, we know that [MATH: |\mathbb{N}| = \aleph_0.] So, [MATH: |A \cup \mathbb{Z}| = \aleph_0 = |\mathbb{N}|.]

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

Content:
Recall that any rational number can be written as [MATH: \dfrac{m}{n},] where [MATH: m,n \in \mathbb{Z}.] This means that any rational number can be defined using a pair of integers:

Content:
[MATH: (m, n) \in \mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}]

Content:
This, in turn, means that [MATH: \mathbb{Q}] can be injectively embedded into the Cartesian product [MATH: \mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z},] and we already know that [MATH: \mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}] is countably infinite.

Content:
Therefore, we have the following theorem:

Content:
> The set of rational numbers is countably infinite, i.e.,
> [MATH: |\mathbb{Q}| = \aleph_0.]

Content:
Let's describe how we can "count" all the elements of the set [MATH: \mathbb{Q}^+,] the set of all positive rationals. We'll then use this to construct a bijection from [MATH: \mathbb N] to [MATH: \mathbb Q.]

Content:
First, we write down the elements of [MATH: \mathbb Q^+] in an infinite array that extends forever to the right and bottom, as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/3358bc21ef5af6417d570d04aa028a1f]

Content:
We skip any equivalent fraction representations if the corresponding number appears somewhere in the previous rows. For example, notice that [MATH: \dfrac{2}{2}=\dfrac11 = 1,] so we can skip this in the second row of the table.

Content:
Now, we can traverse the array in the manner shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/26e52205ee123266951f295e6490762e]

Content:
By assigning each natural number [MATH: n] to the [MATH: n]-th distinct fraction encountered in this path, we define a bijection [MATH: f: \mathbb N\to \mathbb Q^+] between [MATH: \mathbb{N}] and [MATH: \mathbb{Q}^+.]

Content:
[MATH: f(1)|= (1)/(1) = 1; f(2)|= (2)/(1) = 2; f(3)|= (1)/(2); f(4)|= (1)/(3); ⋮]

Content:
Finally, we can use this to construct a bijection [MATH: g: \mathbb N\to \mathbb Q] as follows:

Content:
[MATH: g(1)|= 0; g(2)|= f(1) = 1; g(3)|= − f(1) = − 1; g(4)|= f(2) = 2; g(5)|= − f(2) = − 2; g(6)|= f(3) = (1)/(2); ⋮]

Content:
Or, more compactly:

Content:
[MATH: {0,|n = 1; f((1)/(2)n),|neven; − f((1)/(2)(n − 1)),|n > 1and odd]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
A set [MATH: A] is called countably infinite (or denumerable) if it has the same cardinality as the set of natural numbers.
[MATH: |A| = |\mathbb{N}|]
In other words, [MATH: A] is countably infinite if there exists a bijection between [MATH: A] and the set of natural numbers [MATH: \mathbb{N}.] Elements of a countably infinite set can be listed as a sequence indexed by natural numbers:

Content:
[MATH: a_1, \: a_2, \: \ldots, \: a_n, \: \ldots]

Content:
A set is countable if it is either finite or countably infinite.

Content:
The cardinality of the natural numbers (i.e., all countably infinite sets) is denoted by [MATH: \aleph_0,] which reads as "aleph-zero" or "aleph-null."

Content:
[MATH: |\mathbb{N}| = \aleph_0]

Content:
Aleph-null is the smallest infinite cardinality in the following sense:

Content:
> Any subset of a countably infinite set is either finite or countably infinite.

Content:
Consequently, any infinite subset of a countably infinite set is countably infinite.

Content:
Finally, a set is called uncountable if it's infinite but not countable (i.e., there is no bijection between [MATH: \mathbb{N}] and this set). We will see examples of uncountable sets in future lessons.

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: The Cardinality of the Integers

Content:
Now, let's consider the set of integers:

Content:
[MATH: \mathbb{Z} = \big\{ \ldots, -3, \: -2, \: -1, \: 0 , \: 1, \: 2, \: 3, \: \ldots \big\}]

Content:
Since the elements of [MATH: \mathbb{Z}] can be written in a sequence as

Content:
[MATH: \mathbb{Z} = \big\{ 0, \: 1, \: -1, \: 2, \: -2, \: 3, \: -3, \: \ldots \big\},]

Content:
the set is countably infinite, i.e.,
[MATH: |\mathbb{Z}| = \aleph_0.]

Content:
The diagram below illustrates how to "count" through the entire set of integers:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/45f4052c4b634a4089d6a4c352b0af60]

Content:
Algebraically, the bijection [MATH: f: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z}] shown above can be defined as follows:

Content:
[MATH: {(n)/(2),|if [math]n[/math] is even; (1 − n)/(2),|if [math]n[/math] is odd]

Content:
Note: Any two-way infinite sequence, like the set of integers, can always be represented as a one-way infinite sequence:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/6792840ced0fd680fe14e81d779f6f5e]

---

Item 3 — Example: Identifying Finite, Countably Infinite, and Countable Sets

Example Prompt:
Which of the following statements about the set [MATH: A = \{ (-2)^n \mid n \in \mathbb{N} \}] are true?

1. [MATH: A] is finite
2. [MATH: A] is countably infinite
3. [MATH: A] is countable
4. [MATH: A] is uncountable

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
A set [MATH: A] is countably infinite (or denumerable) if [MATH: |A| = |\mathbb{N}|.] A set is countable if it is either finite or countably infinite.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false. The set [MATH: A] has infinitely many elements.
- Statement II is true. Indeed,
[MATH: A|= {(− 2)^{n}∣n ∈ N}; = {− 2, 4, − 8, 16, − 32…}]
can be represented as a (one-way infinite) sequence. So, it's countably infinite (or denumerable).
- Statement III is true since any countably infinite set is also countable.
- Statement IV is false since statement III is true.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

---

Item 6 — Tutorial: Unions of Countable Sets

Content:
Recall that any infinite subset of a countably infinite set is countably infinite. So, we have the following result concerning intersections of countably infinite sets:

Content:
> The intersection of two countably infinite sets is either finite or countably infinite.

Content:
We also have the following result concerning unions of countably infinite sets:

Content:
> The union of two countably infinite sets is countably infinite.

Content:
This property can be generalized to the union of any number of countably infinite sets and even to the union of countably many countably infinite sets:

Content:
> The union of countably many countably infinite sets is countably infinite.

Content:
We can express this result as follows:

Content:
> If [MATH: |A_i| = \aleph_0] for all natural [MATH: i,] then [MATH: \displaystyle \bigg| \bigcup_{i=1}^\infty A_i \bigg| = \aleph_0.]

Content:
If we combine "fewer" sets (e.g., a finite number), or if some of the [MATH: A_i]'s are finite, the resulting union must also be countable.

---

Item 7 — Example: Identifying the Cardinality of a Union of Sets

Example Prompt:
[MATH: A = \{ 9-x^2=0 \mid x \in \Bbb Q \}]

Given the set [MATH: A] above, which of the following statements are true?

1. [MATH: |A| = 2]
2. [MATH: |A| = |\mathbb{Z}|]
3. [MATH: |A \cup \mathbb{Z}| =|\mathbb{N}|]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Recall that the union of a finite set and a countably infinite set is countably infinite.

Also, note that

- [MATH: A =\{-3, 3\}] is finite with [MATH: |A|=2,] and
- [MATH: \mathbb{N}] and [MATH: \mathbb{Z}] are countably infinite with the same cardinality.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. The set [MATH: A] is finite with [MATH: |A|=2.]
- Statement II is false. The set [MATH: A] is finite with [MATH: |A|=2.] On the other hand, [MATH: \mathbb{Z}] is infinite with [MATH: |\mathbb{Z}|=\aleph_0.] So,
[MATH: | A | =2 \neq \aleph_0 = |\mathbb{Z}|.]
- Statement III is true. The set [MATH: A] is finite, while [MATH: |\mathbb{Z}| = \aleph_0.] As a result, [MATH: |A \cup \mathbb{Z}| = \aleph_0.] On the other hand, we know that [MATH: |\mathbb{N}| = \aleph_0.] So,
[MATH: |A \cup \mathbb{Z}| = \aleph_0 = |\mathbb{N}|.]

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

---

Item 10 — Tutorial: Cartesian Products of Countable Sets

Content:
The Cartesian product of two countably infinite sets is countably infinite. Furthermore, this property can be generalized to any finite number of factors:

Content:
> The Cartesian product of a finite number of countably infinite sets is countably infinite.

Content:
We can express this as follows:

Content:
> If [MATH: |A_i| = \aleph_0] for [MATH: i=1,2,\ldots,n,] then [MATH: \displaystyle \big| A_1 \times A_2 \times \cdots \times A_n \big| = \aleph_0.]

Content:
Let's demonstrate why this is true for the case of two factors, [MATH: A] and [MATH: B.]

Content:
- Since [MATH: A] is countably infinite, it can be represented as a (one-way infinite) sequence, as illustrated below.

Item 11 — Tutorial: The Cardinality of the Rational Numbers

Content:
Recall that any rational number can be written as [MATH: \dfrac{m}{n},] where [MATH: m,n \in \mathbb{Z}.] This means that any rational number can be defined using a pair of integers:

Content:
[MATH: (m, n) \in \mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}]

Content:
This, in turn, means that [MATH: \mathbb{Q}] can be injectively embedded into the Cartesian product [MATH: \mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z},] and we already know that [MATH: \mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}] is countably infinite.

Content:
Therefore, we have the following theorem:

Content:
> The set of rational numbers is countably infinite, i.e.,
> [MATH: |\mathbb{Q}| = \aleph_0.]

Content:
Let's describe how we can "count" all the elements of the set [MATH: \mathbb{Q}^+,] the set of all positive rationals. We'll then use this to construct a bijection from [MATH: \mathbb N] to [MATH: \mathbb Q.]

Content:
First, we write down the elements of [MATH: \mathbb Q^+] in an infinite array that extends forever to the right and bottom, as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/3358bc21ef5af6417d570d04aa028a1f]

Content:
We skip any equivalent fraction representations if the corresponding number appears somewhere in the previous rows. For example, notice that [MATH: \dfrac{2}{2}=\dfrac11 = 1,] so we can skip this in the second row of the table.

Content:
Now, we can traverse the array in the manner shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/26e52205ee123266951f295e6490762e]

Content:
By assigning each natural number [MATH: n] to the [MATH: n]-th distinct fraction encountered in this path, we define a bijection [MATH: f: \mathbb N\to \mathbb Q^+] between [MATH: \mathbb{N}] and [MATH: \mathbb{Q}^+.]

Content:
[MATH: f(1)|= (1)/(1) = 1; f(2)|= (2)/(1) = 2; f(3)|= (1)/(2); f(4)|= (1)/(3); ⋮]

Content:
Finally, we can use this to construct a bijection [MATH: g: \mathbb N\to \mathbb Q] as follows:

Content:
[MATH: g(1)|= 0; g(2)|= f(1) = 1; g(3)|= − f(1) = − 1; g(4)|= f(2) = 2; g(5)|= − f(2) = − 2; g(6)|= f(3) = (1)/(2); ⋮]

Content:
Or, more compactly:

Content:
[MATH: {0,|n = 1; f((1)/(2)n),|neven; − f((1)/(2)(n − 1)),|n > 1and odd]

Item 12 — Example: Identifying the Cardinality of a Cartesian Product

Example Prompt:
Consider the following sets:

[MATH: A = \{ x \in \mathbb{R} \mid \: \cos x =1 \}, \qquad
B = \mathbb{Q}]
Which of the following statements is true?

1. [MATH: A \times B] is uncountable.
2. [MATH: A \times B] is finite
3. [MATH: A \times B] is countably infinite

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The Cartesian product of a finite number of countable sets is countable. In particular, if at least one of the factors is countably infinite, then the resulting product is countably infinite.

- The set [MATH: A=\{0, 2\pi, -2\pi, 4\pi, -4\pi, \ldots\}] is countably infinite. So, it can be represented as a (one-way infinite) sequence.

[IMG: /graphics/af29884c90d9821c1fbfbce645ba83cc]

- The set [MATH: B = \mathbb{Q}] is countably infinite. So, it can be represented as a (one-way infinite) sequence.

[IMG: /graphics/82485a91bb50fe6f483411078c5d05a3]

Therefore, [MATH: A \times B] is countably infinite. So, the correct answer is "III only."

Item 15 — Tutorial: The Arithmetic of Aleph-Zero

Content:
Given two finite, non-overlapping sets of cardinalities [MATH: m] and [MATH: n,] the (disjoint) union of these sets has cardinality [MATH: m+n.]

Content:
For example, to compute [MATH: 2+2,] we can take [MATH: 2] objects and add [MATH: 2] more objects. As a result, we get [MATH: 4] objects:

Content:
[MATH: \large
\underbrace{\square \, \square}_{2} + \underbrace{\square \, \square}_{2} = \underbrace{\square \, \square \, \square \, \square}_{4}]

Content:
This is how we learn to add natural numbers in the first place.
Now, using this analogy, we can define rules of arithmetic involving [MATH: \aleph_0.]

Content:
For example:

Content:
- The union of a finite set and a countably infinite set is countably infinite. In other words, for any finite [MATH: n \in \mathbb{N},] we have
[MATH: n + \aleph_0 = \aleph_0 + n = \aleph_0.]
- The union of two countably infinite sets is countably infinite. So,
[MATH: \aleph_0 + \aleph_0 = \aleph_0.]
- The union of a finite or countable collection of countably infinite sets is countably infinite. So,
[MATH: \underbrace{\aleph_0 + \aleph_0 + \ldots + \aleph_0 + \ldots}_{\textrm{countably many times}} = \aleph_0.]
- The Cartesian product of a finite set and a countably infinite set is countably infinite. In other words, for any finite [MATH: n \in \mathbb{N},] we have
[MATH: n \cdot \aleph_0 = \aleph_0 \cdot n = \aleph_0.]
- The Cartesian product of two countably infinite sets is countably infinite. So,
[MATH: \aleph_0 \cdot \aleph_0 = \aleph_0.]
- The Cartesian product of finitely many countably infinite sets is countably infinite. So,
[MATH: \underbrace{\aleph_0 \cdot \aleph_0 \cdot \cdots \cdot \aleph_0}_{\textrm{finitely many times}} = \aleph_0.]
